newsitem.title: USA: Boston Fed's Minehan sanguine on US '97 outlook.
newsitem.headline: Boston Fed's Minehan sanguine on US '97 outlook.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Cathy Minehan said on Tuesday the U.S. economic outlook is more sanguine in 1997 than it was in 1996, a year she described as close to "economic nirvana."
"Economic nirvana was approached in 1996," Minehan told the Greater Hartford Chamber of Commerce. "At this point, anyway, the outlook for 1997 seems more sanguine."
To support the upbeat outlook, Minehan cited forecasters' consensus expecting the U.S. Gross Domestic Product to "expand near its long-run sustainable pace of 2.0 to 2.5 percent."
Minehan said the forecast implies "the unemployment rate will remain relatively stable at or near its recent low levels."
One key factor in the upbeat economic outlook is that "consumption should remain healthy," although, in a repeat of 1996, "government spending and net exports could act as a drag on the economy.
Minehan expected net exports to remain a drag due "to the effects of a stronger dollar and prospects for only moderate growth in many of our trading partners."

The Boston Fed president, however, pointed out there still are risks to the U.S. economy, such as "the rising burden of debt servicing for the consumer, including the rising deliquency rates on consumer debt."

But Minehan also saw such risk partly offset by the fact that, "on the upside, the moderate level of long-term interest rates seen so far in this expansion may support more strength in interest-sensitive sectors than expected."
Minehan stressed "even with this balanced growth outlook, inflation risk cannot be overlooked," as "labor resources are strained" by an unemployment rate below 5.5 percent.
Minehan acknowledged productivity may be mismeasured, mainly in the service sector, and that labor markets' tighteness may be overstated.
However, she reiterated a theme familiar among U.S. policymakers -- that the Fed should not err on the side of leniency regarding inflation.

"The Federal Reserve's pursuit of low, stable rates of inflation over the last 15 years or so has been a key factor in supporting economic growth," Minehan pointed out. "I, for one, would be loathe to give up on the success on the inflation front that has been achieved to date."
Minehan also cautioned that, while "theories being offered for inflation remaining contained have some validity... they may also be reflecting remporary rather than permanent conditions."
